blogs.title: When Expert Testimony Fails: The Federal Circuit’s Threshold for Substantial Evidence in Patent Infringement
blogs.description: This post dissects the court’s analysis of Dr. Wells’ expert testimony, focusing on how contradictory and vague expert evidence can undermine a jury’s finding of infringement. It will explore the standards for “substantial evidence” and “reasonable juror” under Fifth Circuit law, compare this case to prior Federal Circuit decisions on expert reliability, and discuss the implications for patent litigators in crafting and defending expert reports.

blogs.title: Claim Construction vs. Claim Scope: Why the ‘Three Signals’ Amendment Didn't Disavow Two‑Signal Devices
blogs.description: An examination of the court’s reasoning that Finesse’s amendment to require three separately identifiable signals did not constitute a clear disavowal of two‑signal implementations. The article will analyze claim amendment jurisprudence, the Cont’l Circuits v. Intel standard, and the broader impact on how patentees can shape claim scope without unintentionally narrowing their own coverage.

blogs.title: The Perils of Mapping Patent Limitations to Complex Technical Documents: Lessons from the ’775 Multiplication Dispute
blogs.description: A deep dive into the difficulty of aligning patent claim language—specifically the seven third‑order multiplications—to the technical descriptions in a Nokia document. The post will assess the court’s treatment of extrinsic evidence, the need for clear functional mapping, and how future patent drafts can avoid ambiguous “separately identifiable” language that invites litigation over interpretation.

blogs.title: Damages Vacated: How a Complete JMOL Reversal Forces Courts to Re‑Think Patent Damage Calculations
blogs.description: This article explores the consequences of the Federal Circuit vacating a $166 million award after reversing the infringement findings. It will discuss the relationship between infringement determinations and damages, the abuse‑of‑discretion standard for new‑trial motions, and strategic considerations for parties seeking or defending large patent verdicts.
